deck.title: Periodicity of Chemical Properties of the Elements in Period 3

front_blocks.md: What products form when sodium reacts with cold water, and what is the pH of the solution?

back_blocks.md: Sodium reacts with cold water to form **sodium hydroxide** and **hydrogen** gas: 2Na (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g). The solution is strongly alkaline (pH 14).

front_blocks.md: Define **oxidation number**.

back_blocks.md: An **oxidation number** is a positive or negative integer assigned to an atom in a compound that represents its apparent charge, based on electronegativity-based rules for electron assignment.

front_blocks.md: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>?

back_blocks.md: The oxidation number of phosphorus in P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is **+5**. The 10 oxygen atoms contribute 10 × (−2) = −20, and the 4 phosphorus atoms account for +20 in total (+20 ÷ 4 = +5 each).

front_blocks.md: Describe the reaction of P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> with water.

front_blocks.md: Compare the reactions of Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO with water, including the pH of solutions formed.

back_blocks.md: **Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** reacts with water to form NaOH (aq), giving a strongly alkaline solution (pH 12–14). **MgO** reacts with water to form Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq), giving a weakly alkaline solution (pH 8–10), as magnesium hydroxide is only slightly soluble.

front_blocks.md: Define **amphoteric**.

back_blocks.md: An **amphoteric** substance is one that can act as both an acid and a base. **Aluminium oxide** and **aluminium hydroxide** are amphoteric Period 3 compounds.

front_blocks.md: Why do NaCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub> dissolve in water without reacting with it?

back_blocks.md: NaCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub> have **giant ionic structures**. Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions, hydrating them and breaking down the lattice — no chemical reaction occurs, only dissolving.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> exists as an ionic giant lattice at room temperature.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Anhydrous **AlCl**<sub>**3**</sub> is **covalent** and exists as the dimer **Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**Cl**<sub>**6**</sub>. It only behaves ionically when dissolved in aqueous solution, where it dissociates into Al<sup>3+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
SiO<sub>2</sub> is a basic oxide because it has a giant covalent structure.

**SiO**<sub>**2**</sub> is an **acidic** oxide. Its giant covalent bonding means it has high melting points, but the acid-base character is determined by the electronegativity of Si relative to oxygen, which leads to covalent bonding and acidic behaviour.

front_blocks.md: Define **hydrolysis**.

back_blocks.md: **Hydrolysis** is a chemical reaction in which a compound reacts with water and is broken down. In Period 3 chemistry, covalent chlorides such as SiCl<sub>4</sub> and PCl<sub>5</sub> undergo hydrolysis to produce HCl gas.

front_blocks.md: Why do the oxides of Na and Mg produce alkaline solutions in water, while those of P and S produce acidic solutions?

back_blocks.md: Na and Mg oxides are **ionically bonded**. Their oxide ions (O<sup>2-</sup>) react with water to form OH<sup>-</sup> ions, giving alkaline solutions. P and S oxides are **covalently bonded** and react with water to form acids (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) that donate H<sup>+</sup> ions.

Both **H**<sub>**3**</sub>**PO**<sub>**4**</sub> and dissolved **HCl** are acidic, giving the solution a pH around 2.

front_blocks.md: Explain why adding water to AlCl<sub>3</sub> produces an acidic solution.

back_blocks.md: The highly charged **Al****<sup>3+</sup>** ion becomes hydrated. Its strong charge **polarises** the O–H bonds in the coordinated water molecules, making it easier for one water molecule to release an **H****<sup>+</sup>** ion into solution. This gives the solution its **acidic** character (pH < 7).

front_blocks.md: How does the electronegativity of oxygen compared to Period 3 metals explain why Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO are ionic?

back_blocks.md: Oxygen has an electronegativity of 3.5, much higher than Na (0.9) and Mg (1.2). The large difference means electrons are **transferred** from the metal to oxygen, forming **ionic bonds** in Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO.

front_blocks.md: Define **electronegativity**.

back_blocks.md: **Electronegativity** is the power of an atom to draw the bonding electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

front_blocks.md: Why does electronegativity increase across Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Across Period 3, **nuclear charge** increases while **shielding** stays roughly constant (electrons are added to the same shell). This means the nucleus attracts bonding electrons more strongly, increasing **electronegativity** from Na to Cl.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Aluminium is a better electrical conductor than sodium because it donates 3 electrons to the delocalised sea.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

**Aluminium** donates 3 electrons per atom to the delocalised sea, creating more charge carriers and stronger **metallic bonding** than sodium (1 electron) or magnesium (2 electrons), making Al the best conductor of the three.

back_blocks.md: Across Period 3, bonding changes from **metallic** in Na, Mg and Al to **covalent** in Si, P, S and Cl.

front_blocks.md: Why cannot phosphorus, sulfur or chlorine conduct electricity?

back_blocks.md: P, S and Cl exist as **simple molecules** with only weak **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole** forces between them. They have no **delocalised electrons**, so there are no mobile charge carriers to carry an electric current.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Silicon has a simple molecular structure similar to phosphorus.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

**Silicon** has a **giant molecular** (covalent) structure in which each Si atom is covalently bonded to four neighbouring Si atoms. This is fundamentally different from phosphorus, which exists as simple P<sub>4</sub> molecules.

front_blocks.md: What is the molecular formula of phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine in their elemental forms?

back_blocks.md: Phosphorus exists as **P**<sub>**4**</sub>, sulfur as **S**<sub>**8**</sub> and chlorine as **Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>. These are all simple molecular structures with strong covalent bonds within the molecules and weak **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole** forces between them.

front_blocks.md: Explain why Al<sup>3+</sup> forms stronger metallic bonds than Na<sup>+</sup>.

back_blocks.md: **Al**<sup>**3+**</sup> has a higher ionic charge and contributes more delocalised electrons (3 per atom) than **Na**<sup>**+**</sup> (1 per atom). The greater electrostatic forces between the Al<sup>3+</sup> ions and the larger 'sea' of electrons result in stronger metallic bonding.

front_blocks.md: Define **giant ionic structure**.

back_blocks.md: A **giant ionic structure** is a three-dimensional lattice of oppositely charged ions held together by strong **electrostatic forces**. Examples in Period 3 include NaCl, MgCl<sub>2</sub>, Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO.

cards.front_md: Define **giant ionic structure**.
cards.back_md: A **giant ionic structure** is a three-dimensional lattice of oppositely charged ions held together by strong **electrostatic forces**. Examples in Period 3 include NaCl, MgCl<sub>2</sub>, Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO.

front_blocks.md: Describe the trend in bonding and structure of the Period 3 oxides from Na<sub>2</sub>O to SO<sub>3</sub>.

back_blocks.md: From Na<sub>2</sub>O to SO<sub>3</sub>, the bonding changes from **ionic** (Na<sub>2</sub>O, MgO) through mixed ionic-covalent (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) to **covalent** (SiO<sub>2</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>, SO<sub>3</sub>). The structure changes from **giant ionic** to giant covalent to **simple molecular**.

cards.front_md: Describe the trend in bonding and structure of the Period 3 oxides from Na<sub>2</sub>O to SO<sub>3</sub>.
cards.back_md: From Na<sub>2</sub>O to SO<sub>3</sub>, the bonding changes from **ionic** (Na<sub>2</sub>O, MgO) through mixed ionic-covalent (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) to **covalent** (SiO<sub>2</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>, SO<sub>3</sub>). The structure changes from **giant ionic** to giant covalent to **simple molecular**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
PCl<sub>5</sub> has a giant ionic structure.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**PCl**<sub>**5**</sub> has **covalent** bonding and a **simple molecular** structure. It undergoes hydrolysis when added to water, unlike ionic chlorides which simply dissolve.

front_blocks.md: Why do covalent Period 3 chlorides react more vigorously with water than ionic ones?

back_blocks.md: Covalent chlorides such as SiCl<sub>4</sub> and PCl<sub>5</sub> are **hydrolysed** by water, breaking covalent bonds. Ionic chlorides such as NaCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub> simply **dissolve** as their ions are already separated. Hydrolysis requires bond breaking and is more vigorous.

front_blocks.md: SiO<sub>2</sub> has a **..........**  covalent structure, while P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> have **..........**  molecular structures.

back_blocks.md: SiO<sub>2</sub> has a **giant** covalent structure, while P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> have **simple** molecular structures.

cards.front_md: SiO<sub>2</sub> has a **..........**  covalent structure, while P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> have **..........**  molecular structures.
cards.back_md: SiO<sub>2</sub> has a **giant** covalent structure, while P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> have **simple** molecular structures.

front_blocks.md: What is the chemical bonding and structure of Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>?

back_blocks.md: **Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**Cl**<sub>**6**</sub> (anhydrous aluminium chloride) has **covalent** bonding and a **simple molecular** structure, existing as a dimer. This is in contrast to NaCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub>, which are ionic with giant lattice structures.
